summaries.example: Imagine a red ball on a table. It can become blue later, but at this moment, in the same way, it cannot be both completely red and completely not red. Aristotle also says that people show this idea in their actions: they avoid stepping into a hole because they treat the hole as really being there.
summaries.summary: Aristotle’s principle of non-contradiction says that one thing cannot both have and not have the same feature at the same time and in the same way. A cup can be warm now and cool later, but it cannot be both warm and not warm in exactly the same respect at exactly the same moment. Aristotle believed this principle is the firmest starting point for thinking. We cannot prove it in the usual way, because any proof or conversation already depends on keeping meanings and claims apart. Instead, Aristotle challenges someone who rejects it to say one definite thing. If the person uses words with no stable meaning, discussion stops. If the person speaks clearly, the person seems to accept some difference between what is and what is not. Aristotle also points to action. Someone who avoids a cliff acts as if the cliff is real and dangerous, not as if every opposite possibility is equally true. He considers disagreements caused by changing appearances, such as something seeming sweet to one person and bitter to another. He argues that we can still ask which sense, condition, or informed judgment is best suited to the question. Scholars continue to disagree about exactly which version of the principle Aristotle meant to establish and how much his argument depends on his view that things have essential natures.
key_ideas: Aristotle thought the principle of non-contradiction was needed for learning, science, and ordinary conversation.
The rule applies to the same thing, at the same time, and in the same respect.
Aristotle discussed things, beliefs, and statements: these are three connected ways to understand non-contradiction.
People may say confusing things, but their clear speech and practical actions often show that they rely on this principle.
Different appearances do not automatically mean that every opinion is equally correct.
summaries.why_it_matters: The idea helps explain why clear words, careful reasoning, science, and shared decisions matter. If every claim and its opposite were equally acceptable in the same situation, it would be hard to learn, solve problems, or decide how to act. Aristotle’s discussion also invites us to examine the limits of certainty and the difference between how things seem and how they are.

important_terms.definition: A rule saying that the same thing cannot have a property and lack that property at the same time and in the same respect.
A feature that tells what something is, rather than just what it happens to be like.
A feature that can change while the thing stays what it is, such as hair color.
A statement that says something about something else, such as “the ball is red.”

questions_to_think_about: Can something be one way now and a different way later without being a contradiction?
Why must a word have a reasonably clear meaning for a conversation to work?
Do our actions show what we really believe?
If two people see colors differently, how might we investigate what is happening?

summaries.example: Suppose a metal bar is actually hot but could later become cold. Its being potentially cold does not contradict its being actually hot. A contradiction would arise only if the very same bar were actually hot and actually not hot at the same time and in the same respect. This example shows why Aristotle distinguishes actuality from possibility and why qualifications about identity, time, and respect matter.
summaries.summary:
The SEP entry examines Aristotle’s defense of the principle of non-contradiction, especially in Metaphysics IV. The principle can be understood in at least three ways: as a claim about incompatible properties in things, as a claim about contradictory beliefs, and as a claim about opposing assertions and truth. The text emphasizes that these formulations do not straightforwardly settle whether Aristotle is defending the world’s structure, rational belief, or the impossibility of intelligible denial.

Aristotle calls non-contradiction the firmest first principle and a common axiom of the sciences. It is not demonstrated from prior premises, because any demonstration would already rely on distinctions that the principle supports. His alternative is an elenctic or self-refutational strategy. A person who rejects the principle must still signify something definite, use language, and choose actions. Yet doing so seems to require treating some things as one way rather than its opposite. The details are controversial, especially whether this establishes the truth of the ontological principle or merely its indispensability for thought and discourse.

Aristotle’s defense is tied to essentialism. Substances or kinds have natures, while accidental features can change without destroying the thing. This framework helps explain why a subject can remain the same while becoming pale rather than dark, but it also raises questions about whether non-contradiction depends on Aristotle’s particular metaphysics. Aristotle further responds to conflicts among appearances by distinguishing changes in observers, species, senses, and conditions. He denies that such conflicts make all opinions equally reliable; the relevant sense or an expert judgment may have greater authority.

key_ideas: The entry distinguishes ontological, doxastic, and semantic formulations of non-contradiction, while noting that scholars dispute their exact relation.
Aristotle treats the principle as a common and exceptionally firm first principle. It cannot receive an ordinary demonstration, since demonstration itself depends on it.
His elenctic method is not simply a formal proof. It pressures a denier to use meaningful language, make distinctions, and engage in action that appears to presuppose the principle.

Aristotle connects non-contradiction with essentialism: meaningful predication requires subjects that are more than loose bundles of accidental features. The strength and scope of this connection remain debated.
Conflicting appearances motivate relativist or skeptical conclusions, but Aristotle argues that different observers, senses, and conditions are not automatically equally authoritative.
Modern dialetheists and paraconsistent logicians reopen questions about whether contradictions can be true and whether one contradiction must make every claim follow.
summaries.why_it_matters: Non-contradiction stands at the meeting point of logic, metaphysics, language, science, and practical reasoning. It asks what must already be in place for disagreement to be meaningful and inquiry to begin. The entry also shows that a seemingly basic logical rule has consequences for realism, skepticism, relativism, ethics, and politics. Contemporary debates about true contradictions and paraconsistent logic demonstrate that Aristotle’s question remains open to challenge, even when his own position is clear.

important_terms.definition: Aristotle’s central principle that the same thing cannot possess and fail to possess the same property simultaneously and in the same respect.
The version concerning what exists: incompatible properties cannot belong to the same thing under the relevant qualifications.
The version concerning belief; it may mean that contradictory belief is impossible or that holding it is irrational.
The version concerning language and truth: opposing assertions cannot both be true at the same time.
A basic starting point shared by the sciences, rather than a conclusion derived from an earlier premise.
A strategy that shows a position is unstable by getting its defender to commit to claims that conflict with the position.
The view that members of kinds have defining natures, while changeable features such as color are nonessential.
The view that some contradictions can be true; it is a modern challenge to Aristotle’s position.

questions_to_think_about: Is Aristotle trying to prove that non-contradiction is true, or only that it cannot coherently be rejected?
Does meaningful speech require stable essences, or can reference work without Aristotelian essentialism?
When appearances conflict, what makes one observer, sense, or method more authoritative?
Can someone act as if a claim is true without actually believing it?
Would a paraconsistent logic challenge Aristotle’s argument, or only some of its consequences?

summaries.example: A student says, “This map is accurate and not accurate.” That might not be a real contradiction if the map is accurate for roads but not for hiking trails, or accurate today but outdated next year. Aristotle would ask whether the same map is being discussed, at the same time, and in the same respect. The extra details help us decide whether the two claims truly oppose each other.
summaries.summary:
Aristotle’s principle of non-contradiction says that the same thing cannot both have and not have the same feature at the same time and in the same respect. The phrase “in the same respect” matters. A person can be a baseball pitcher and stand beside a pitcher used for drinks, because the word has different meanings. A table can be red now and possibly become non-red later, but it cannot be actually red and actually non-red at the same moment in the same way.

The entry discusses three related versions. One concerns things in the world. Another concerns what it is possible or reasonable to believe. A third concerns whether opposite statements can both be true. Scholars disagree about which version Aristotle is mainly defending and how the versions support one another. The belief version is especially difficult because people sometimes have inconsistent beliefs. It may therefore be a rule about rational belief rather than a description of what people always think.

Aristotle calls non-contradiction the firmest first principle shared by all scientific inquiry. He says it cannot be demonstrated from an earlier, firmer premise. Instead, he uses an elenctic challenge. Someone who rejects the principle must still say something meaningful. But to signify one definite thing, the speaker must use a stable meaning and identify a subject about which something is said. Aristotle argues that refusing this challenge would make speech and inquiry collapse.

He also connects the principle to essentialism, his view that kinds of things have defining natures. key_ideas: Aristotle’s principle concerns reality, belief, and true statements, not just one narrow kind of contradiction.
He thinks the principle cannot be proved like an ordinary theorem because every proof already needs clear differences between claims.
To argue with someone who rejects the principle, Aristotle asks that person to use words with a definite meaning. Without that, there is no clear position to discuss.
Aristotle connects the principle with essence and accident. A person can change hair color without ceasing to be a person, but changing from a person into something else would be a deeper change.
Different people or animals may experience the same thing differently. Aristotle says this does not show that all appearances or opinions are equally trustworthy.
The entry presents later challenges, including the idea that some contradictions might be true and that logic need not make every conclusion follow from one contradiction.
summaries.why_it_matters: This issue matters because reasoning together requires more than having opinions. We need stable meanings, ways to distinguish better evidence from worse evidence, and some agreement that a claim cannot simply be both true and false in exactly the same way. Aristotle’s argument also helps us see why disagreements about perception, reality, and language remain important in philosophy.

important_terms.definition: The rule that the same thing cannot both have and lack the same feature at the same time and in the same respect.
A basic starting rule used in thinking and in all the sciences.
A way of challenging a claim by showing that the speaker’s own words or actions depend on the claim being rejected.
What a word or statement picks out or means; Aristotle asks an opponent to make this definite.
What makes a thing the kind of thing it is, as opposed to a changeable feature like color or temperature.
A changeable feature that belongs to something without defining what it is.
The view that truth depends entirely on how things appear to each person.

questions_to_think_about: What makes two apparently opposite statements genuine contradictions?
Why might a proof of the first principle be impossible?
Can a person reject a rule while still using it in conversation?
Are all points of view equally reliable when people disagree?
What is the difference between something changing and something ceasing to be what it is?
